summary: Clear, readable, batteries-included language dominating scripting, backend web services, data science, and modern AI.

rows.means: outputs text and values to standard output
rows.consequence: Accepts any number of objects, converts them via str(), separates them with sep, and appends end (defaults to newline).

rows.means: defines a reusable function with positional and keyword arguments
rows.consequence: *args captures surplus positional arguments as a tuple; **kwargs captures surplus keyword arguments as a dictionary.

rows.means: returns a single final value / yields items lazily one at a time
rows.consequence: yield turns a function into a memory-efficient generator, allowing streaming iteration over gigabytes of data without storing it all in RAM.

rows.means: conditional branching based on truthy evaluation
rows.consequence: Python treats 0, None, empty collections ([], {}, ''), and False as falsy; everything else evaluates to truthy.

rows.means: iterates directly over any sequence or generator
rows.consequence: No manual index counters needed. Iterates over lists, strings, dictionaries, files, or database cursor streams.

rows.means: generates an immutable arithmetic progression sequence
rows.consequence: Memory efficient: range(1000000) consumes the same tiny constant memory as range(10) because values are generated on-demand.

rows.means: returns the number of items in O(1) constant time
rows.consequence: Python collections store their length directly in memory header structures, so len() never counts elements one by one.

rows.code: List comprehension: [x**2 for x in items if x > 0]
rows.means: concise syntax for filtering and mapping a new list
rows.consequence: Significantly faster than manual for loops with list.append() because the iteration executes at C-speed in the interpreter.

rows.code: Dict comprehension: {k: v for k, v in pairs}
rows.means: builds a dictionary in a single readable expression
rows.consequence: Ideal for inverting mappings or indexing list records: {user['id']: user for user in users}.

rows.means: unnamed, single-expression anonymous function
rows.consequence: Used for quick throwaway operations, such as custom sorting keys: sorted(users, key=lambda u: u['age']).

rows.means: guarantees setup and teardown cleanup even on exceptions
rows.consequence: Automatically calls f.close() when the block exits, preventing file descriptor leaks and database connection exhaustion.

rows.code: try / except SpecificError as e / else / finally
rows.means: handles runtime exceptions cleanly
rows.consequence: Always catch specific exceptions rather than bare except:, which accidentally swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit.

rows.means: explicitly triggers an exception
rows.consequence: Halts the current function and bubbles up to the caller with a descriptive error message and stack trace.

rows.means: defines an object-oriented class with constructor
rows.consequence: self is the explicit reference to the current instance, through which instance attributes and methods are accessed.

rows.means: human-readable text display / unambiguous developer debug string
rows.consequence: __str__ is used by print(); __repr__ should ideally return a valid Python expression recreating the object.

rows.means: exposes a method as an attribute with getter and setter logic
rows.consequence: Allows adding validation or computed calculations to attribute access without breaking existing code that reads obj.attribute.

rows.means: wraps a function to add logging, caching, or authentication
rows.consequence: Syntactic sugar for func = decorator(func). Used everywhere in web frameworks (e.g. @app.get('/'), @login_required).

rows.means: interpolates expressions directly into string literals
rows.consequence: Evaluated at runtime. Supports inline formatting like decimals ({x:.2f}), padding, and debug print ({var=}).

rows.means: extracts sub-sequences or reverses arrays
rows.consequence: list[1:4] gets items at indices 1, 2, 3. list[::-1] returns a reversed copy of the list.

rows.means: yields (index, item) pairs during iteration
rows.consequence: Replaces manual counter variables: for i, val in enumerate(items): print(i, val).

rows.means: aggregates elements from multiple iterables in lockstep
rows.consequence: for name, score in zip(names, scores): pairs elements up; stops as soon as the shortest iterable is exhausted.

rows.means: returns a new sorted list using Timsort algorithm
rows.consequence: Stable O(n log n) sorting algorithm. Use the key parameter to sort by custom object attributes or dictionary keys.

rows.means: checks if at least one item is truthy / checks if all are truthy
rows.consequence: Short-circuits immediately upon determining the outcome: any() stops at the first True; all() stops at the first False.

rows.means: checks if an object is an instance of a class or tuple of classes
rows.consequence: Preferred over type(obj) == class because isinstance correctly handles class inheritance and subclasses.

rows.means: dictionary with default factories / frequency counter
rows.consequence: Counter(words) automatically calculates word frequencies; defaultdict(list) initializes new keys with empty lists without KeyError.

rows.means: automatically generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ for classes
rows.consequence: Eliminates repetitive boilerplate when defining pure data-holding classes: @dataclass class User: id: int; name: str.

rows.code: typing: Optional[T], List[T], Dict[K, V], Union[A, B]
rows.means: type annotations for static analysis tools like mypy
rows.consequence: Provides self-documenting function contracts that can be verified during CI/CD to catch type bugs before production.

rows.means: checks memory identity against the singleton / checks equality
rows.consequence: Always use is None. None is a unique singleton in Python memory; is checks exact identity in pointer memory.

rows.means: boilerplate ensuring code runs only when executed directly
rows.consequence: Prevents test scripts and script execution from triggering when the file is imported as a library module by other files.
